newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's BHP returns to profit growth in Q3.
newsitem.headline: Australia's BHP returns to profit growth in Q3.

text.p: Australian resource giant, the Broken Hill Co Pty Ltd (BHP), staged a strong return from two years of falling profits on Friday, posting a 69.5 percent jump in third quarter net profit.
BHP reported a net profit of A$378 million (US$296 million) for the three months to February 28, up from A$223 million in the previous corresponding period.
It was the mining company's first profit rise since March 1995, when it increased its third quarter net earnings to A$322 million from A$284 million in the previous corresponding period.
The result was struck on an 11.8 percent lift in overall group sales to A$5.14 billion with the company, Australia's largest, maintaining its final dividend at 26 cents a share.
BHP said a doubling in profits from its petroleum division, on the back of higher world oil and gas prices, to A$246 million from A$121 million was largely responsible for its comeback.
The surge in the petroleum division's profits was attributed to an average realised oil price for the quarter of A$31.36 a barrel, up from A$26.30 in the same quarter a year earlier.
"Realised oil prices peaked in January and have since declined," BHP said.
The division's tax expense also fell because of certain tax effects from overseas exploration and a cut in prior period tax provision.
"There was also a net profit of A$16 million from the sale of Gulf of Mexico assets and an Australian exploration permit," it said.

BHP Copper's profits rose to A$145 million from A$88 million, due to higher output, better prices and lower costs, while profits from its steel division rose to A$72 million from A$44 million, stemming from lower costs from an improved manufacturing performance and lower employee numbers.
Investors reacted positively to the result after an initial sell-down, with the stock closing three cents higher at A$17.16 after trading as low as A$17.05 following the announcement.

The result was at the higher end of market expectations, which had centred on a net profit of A$330 million to A$370 million, but analysts said early studies of the profit figure indicated it may not be as strong as it appeared on the surface.
"The result does not appear to be as good as the first cut shows," said a Melbourne-based analyst, who declined to be named.

"There is some asset sales and tax adjustments in the A$378 million number and that brings it back towards the A$330-340 million level, which is probably a bit below the market's expectations," he said.
But analysts said that even so, this did not explain the fall in BHP's share price immediately after the release of the results.
They said it was more likely that the inital drop was related to profit-taking and weakness in the major offshore stock markets on Thursday.
"The market has pushed it up over the last few days, having heard a rumour of a great result," a Sydney-based analyst said.
"It was a good result, but perhaps not as good as some of the rumour-mongers in the market had expected."

BHP managing director John Prescott said the company would now focus on boosting its minerals business in coming months after weather problems negatively impacted on its iron ore and coal operations during the quarter.
The minerals division recorded a profit of A$105 million, up only A$1.0 million from a year earlier.

The company also hoped to finish a mine feasibility study by the end of next year on a nickel deposit on Gag Island in Indonesia. BHP said last year it would hold a 75 percent stake in the venture if a mine was developed with Indonesia's P.T. Aneka Tambang holding the remainder.
